items.description: Luxury Cut: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking By Anthony Smith Oct 29, 2026 The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking St Louis Downtown and Arch – SeanPavonePhoto/Adobe Stock St. Louis Returns to the Top St. Louis has made its way back to the top spot this quarter in the Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking. The top 5 rounds out with Charlottesville, VA; Portland, ME; Bridgeport, CT; and Pittsfield, MA, which took the top spot last quarter. Common themes across the top-ranked markets include low climate risk, lower unemployment rates, and higher levels of buyer demand. Each quarter, Realtor.com and the Wall Street Journal team up to identify the highest-performing and most attractive metro areas for luxury home purchases. We score 60 different luxury housing markets across the country in categories that include supply and demand strength, economic health, and quality of life. This fall’s ranking points to a return to fundamentals: markets with active buyer demand, homes that sell at a steady pace, and low exposure to climate risk moved to the front of the pack, while several lifestyle-driven markets that led earlier this year slipped out of the top 10. Highlights St. Louis climbs from No. 12 to No. 1 , reclaiming the top spot it last held in summer 2025, backed by the lowest cost of living in the ranking, strong buyer demand, and minimal climate risk. Four new entries joined the top 10 : St. Louis, Portland, ME (No. 3), Bridgeport, CT (No. 4), and Detroit (No. 6). Charlottesville, VA, reaches No. 2 , its highest placement yet, extending its run to six straight quarters in the top 10. Four markets exited the top 10 . Boulder, CO, fell from No. 2 to No. 15. San Jose, CA, dropped from No. 3 to No. 37. Santa Fe, NM, slipped from No. 4 to No. 16, and Santa Barbara, CA, moved from No. 10 to No. 17. St. Louis last topped the list in summer 2025 and held the No. 2 spot last fall and at the beginning of this year. Beyond the lower cost of living, the metro also has strong demand and low climate risk. The Midwest market is not often thought of when it comes to luxury, but it has many compelling draws compared to the higher price tags and elevated climate risk that accompany many coastal markets. The starting point for luxury in the St. Louis metro is just over $670,000 as of September, well below the national benchmark of roughly $1.2 million. In fact, a buyer at that national threshold would already be shopping in the top 5% of St. Louis listings, where the 95th percentile starts just under $900,000. Despite the lower price points, million dollar homes typically spend 59 days on the market compared to the 74 days at the national level. Only 3.7% of St. Louis listings are million-dollar homes, while the national share comes in at 12.5%. St. Louis also offers more for your money in the $1 million to $2 million price tier. The median home at that price point in the metro measures 4,430 square feet, compared to 3,016 square feet for the same price tier nationally. Most Expensive Areas in St. Louis Just because the cost of living is lower in St. Louis doesn’t mean there aren’t pricey ZIP codes. Some of the most expensive areas are 63131, covering Des Peres and Frontenac; 63005, covering Chesterfield; and 63073, covering Saint Albans. All three of these ZIP codes have median listing prices above the $1 million mark. Charlottesville Reaches Its Highest Ranking Yet The Charlottesville, VA, metro has been one of the most consistent markets in the quarterly rankings. It has placed in the top 10 for six straight quarters, and this quarter’s No. 2 spot is its highest ranking yet. Some of its top attributes are low unemployment (3.1%), a cost of living below the national average and well below traditional coastal metros, and low climate risk. Luxury buyers in Charlottesville are also seeing more choice. The 90th percentile listing price sits at $1,360,000 as of September, down 5.9% year over year, while the number of million-dollar listings is up 14.6% from a year ago. The metro posted the third-highest buyer demand score in the field and the lowest unemployment rate in the top 10 at 2.7%, a combination that points to a healthy local economy and active buyer interest. Luxury prices have cooled, with the 90th percentile at $1,607,650 as of September, down 9.4% year over year. That adjustment has come alongside more options for buyers: million-dollar homes now make up 21.6% of listings, with their count up 8.8% from a year ago, and those homes are spending a median of 68 days on the market, about three days faster than last year. items.description: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Housing Market Ranking By Hannah Jones Oct 29, 2026 Introduction The summer housing market lacked its usual energy as volatile, generally rising mortgage rates eroded affordability and buyer confidence. Early-year affordability wins gave way to higher housing costs. By the best time to buy , mortgage rates were above 7% , and buyers had to confront challenging financing headwinds even as broader market conditions, including more inventory and signs of seller flexibility , lined up in their favor. The 30-year fixed rate now averages 7.40%, up from 6.27% a year ago. On the same loan, today’s higher rate adds roughly 12% to the, in many cases, already-high monthly payment, enough to put some buyers’ plans on hold. The national picture masks a sharper regional divide . The Northeast and Midwest continue to see relatively strong demand and limited supply, which keeps sellers in the driver’s seat. The South and West are more balanced, with both buyers and sellers having room to negotiate. There is some good news for buyers. Inventory has grown in much of the country, price reductions are more common and asking prices have even softened in many markets. Buyers who can handle higher rates have more room to offset them with a lower price or seller concessions. They can also beat the headline rate by shopping lenders, improving their credit score and making a larger down payment. Planning for rate volatility and building flexibility into their housing budget can help them succeed even in a difficult market. This challenging backdrop gives some context as to why this quarter’s ranking elevates markets where a dollar goes farther. Nineteen of the top 20 markets are in the Midwest and Northeast where, in many cases, prices still pencil out against local incomes. The Fall 2026 WSJ/Realtor.com Housing Market Ranking highlights the markets best positioned to deliver stability, livability and long-term value. Fall 2026 WSJ/Realtor.com Housing Market Ranking Volatile mortgage rates through the summer and into the fall squeezed buyer budgets and many would-be buyers decided to opt out of the market once again. Sellers responded by pricing lower and reducing prices more, but transaction volume still suffered. In this challenging affordability environment, metros that combine lower prices with steady demand, improving supply conditions, and strong quality-of-life fundamentals continue to stand out. The Fall 2026 ranking evaluates the 200 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas using a combination of housing market conditions and broader measures of economic health and livability. Together, these factors highlight markets where buyers are more likely to find balance in an otherwise challenging housing environment. Rank Metro Pop. items.title: Las Vegas multifamily rent pressures persist despite leasing gains
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Las Vegas multifamily market report here.HighlightsLas Vegas multifamily operating conditions remain soft, with elevated vacancy, rising concessions and declining rents. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, but the improved supply-demand balance has yet to translate into rent growth.Stabilized vacancy reached 9.1% at the end of the third quarter, flat from the prior quarter but up 20 basis points from one year earlier. Vacancy remains 30 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month by the end of September, down 1.4% year over year and 0.9% lower than in the prior quarter, the second consecutive quarterly decline.Investment sales volume during the third quarter totaled roughly $209 million across five deals, with Class B properties accounting for four of the five deals. The year-to-date median sale price reached $225,900 per unit.Las Vegas multifamily market overviewLas Vegas multifamily fundamentals remain under pressure despite improved absorption and a slowdown in new deliveries in 2026. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries by roughly 650 units year to date, after trailing them by nearly 1,700 units in 2025. Absorption has already surpassed the full-year 2025 total, supported by continued job growth, while completions have slowed as fewer projects remain under construction. The recovery has been concentrated in the suburbs, where Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of that demand with less than half of the metro’s inventory. Rent growth has been slower to rebound. Asking rents remain below year-ago levels, with the steepest declines in older urban core submarkets, where vacancy is above 10%. By contrast, rents in suburban submarkets remain close to year-ago levels.Investment activity in 2026 has become concentrated in two of the suburban submarkets that are leading the leasing recovery. Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson accounted for roughly three-quarters of metro sales volume through the third quarter, up from 43% in 2025. Third-quarter activity followed the same pattern, with three of the five trades located in those two submarkets. Pricing has remained stable in Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson, with median sale prices near $250,000 per unit in both submarkets, above levels elsewhere in the metro, where recent trades have skewed toward smaller, older properties. The median price across the Las Vegas region has remained near its 2025 level, highlighting the influence of property location on pricing trends.Employment:Area employers added 21,400 jobs year over year. Image Area payrolls increased by 21,400 jobs year over year as of the third quarter of 2026, a gain of 1.8%. Hiring slowed from the first half of the year and held below the 10-year average annual growth rate of 2.4%.Professional and business services remained the leading source of new jobs, adding 10,900 positions and expanding 6.3% year over year. Education and health services added 5,400 jobs, while leisure and hospitality, the largest local employment sector, shed 2,200 positions, a 0.7% decline.Hyve Solutions, a manufacturer of storage and AI computing hardware, is establishing a new production facility in North Las Vegas. The project, the largest of four business expansions approved for state tax incentives in August, is expected to create 240 jobs over the next two years.Forecast: Employers are forecast to add roughly 20,000 jobs in 2026, a 1.7% increase, maintaining a pace similar to 2025. Development and permitting:Developers completed roughly 600 units in the third quarter. Image Developers completed roughly 600 units in the third quarter, all in Central Las Vegas. Year-to-date deliveries total around 2,600 units, down 23% from the same period in 2025. Roughly 6,100 units were under construction at the end of the third quarter, down more than 25% from the end of 2025, which is expected to ease supply pressure on operators heading into 2027. Six active projects in Spring Valley total more than 2,000 units.Multifamily permitting activity is regaining momentum. Developers pulled permits for 1,130 multifamily units in the third quarter, more than double the total from one year earlier.Forecast: Developers are expected to complete roughly 4,000 units in 2026, in line with both the 2025 total and the 10-year average.Vacancy:Vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1% Image Stabilized vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1%, up 20 basis points year over year. Despite the annual increase, net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, pushing vacancy down 30 basis points from year-end 2025.Class B properties account for roughly 70% of net absorption this year, with vacancy flat year over year at 9.0%. Class A vacancy edged up to 8.4%, while Class C, the only tier with negative net absorption in 2026, posted the highest vacancy at 10.0%.Suburban submarkets continue to pull away from the urban core. Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of net absorption this year, each with vacancy below 7.5%. Las Vegas Strip vacancy rose 170 basis points year over year to 12.1%.Forecast: Vacancy is expected to tick up 20 basis points to 9.3% by year-end 2026, though it would remain 10 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Rents:Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month. items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent. items.title: A path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table
items.description: Housing demand has stabilized over the last two weeks as rates have fallen a tad, and we can finally see a clear path back to sub-7% mortgage rates . We survived the crazy month of October, when the 10-year had the potential to close above 5.35%, which would have created a backdrop of bond-escalation selling, sending mortgage rates above 8%. That didn’t happen, of course, as the 10-year yield held that key line! Not only has the 10-year yield now gone below 5% — with mortgage rates closer to 7% than 8% today — but what this month has shown us is that there’s a clear path for sub-7% mortgage rates. Just the move in the last two weeks has stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, so let’s take a look on this Halloween on what needs to happen to get rates lower. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week was Fed week, and even Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said tighter policy has created financial pain for some AI companies. The Federal Reserve has been talking more and more about AI being very inflationary for many weeks now, so naturally, when AI companies are having debt-financing issues, and some are missing on their numbers, the 10-year yield has gone lower even with elevated oil prices and economic data staying firm. However, imagine for a minute that the Iran conflict was over: oil would be trading between $67 and $82. Imagine that the trade war 2.0 doesn’t get worse and you have an AI slowdown; there’s your trinity for lower mortgage rates. Nothing too drastic, but definitely sub-7%, and we’ve all seen what mortgage demand can do when rates drop below 6.64%. So there’s a pathway to 7%, but there’s also a pathway for rates to stay above 7% if the AI story rebounds, the conflict doesn’t end, and the trade war continues. This, of course, would need the economic data to stay very positive, as it has recently. Since Sept. 10, a clear head-and-shoulders pattern has formed in the 10-year yield so what I said above can break that lower and get us sub-7% rates. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multi-year lows. I can’t stress enough how important it is for spreads to be closer to 2% than 3%, since mortgage rates would already be over 8% now if this were not the case. Not only that, it would have been impossible to get mortgage rates near 7% again without a much bigger move lower with the 10-year yield. That said, when the 10-year yield moves lower at times, spreads can widen after a big move up because their job is to compress volatility. Now, this does wear off over time, and we can head lower again. What you don’t want to see is the Fed suddenly changing course and starting a massive rate-hike cycle, or a credit event like the Silicon Valley Bank crisis. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads were flat at 2.23% from week to week. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been over the last three years, given the 10-year yield’s current level: If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.15% today, not 7.27%. If we had the worst levels of 2024, mortgage rates would be 7.77% today. If we had the worst levels of 2025, mortgage rates would be 7.58% today. items.title: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum
items.description: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 29, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Whether you call them “gateway” markets or the “sexy six,” the primary coastal hubs that traditionally attract the majority of domestic and international capital are well represented among the top markets for annual multifamily permitting in September’s data release from the U.S. Census Bureau, and in most cases are dramatically increasing their permitting activity. New York continues to lead the nation for multifamily permitting with 37,691 units permitted in the year-ending September, an increase of more than 13,000 units from last year or a jump of 52.7%. Los Angeles again ranked #2 with about 18,000 units permitted, almost doubling their annual total from one year ago. Washington, DC remained among the top permitting markets at #5 in September, increasing their annual permitting by 47.4% or about 3,900 units, while Seattle slipped to #11 this month but still increased their multifamily permitting total by 36.7% or roughly 2,400 units. Rounding out the “sexy six,” Boston ranked #16 among Realpage’s top 150 markets with a 44.7% annual increase (+2,303 units) to 7,460 units, while the Bay Area markets of San Jose, Oakland and San Francisco ranked well down the list individually but would have ranked #7 with a combined total of 11,543 units permitted, up 46.8% from last year (+5,407 units). Conversely, among the secondary high-growth markets, development activity has stalled or fallen back as top 10 markets Phoenix and Atlanta permitted close to the same amount as last year, while Dallas, Houston, Austin and Miami decreased their permitted unit counts by a combined 11,004 units. Only Raleigh/Durham saw a significant increase in multifamily permitting (+3,153 units) among the non-gateway top 10 markets. Despite declining permitting in four of September’s top 10 markets, their combined total of 148,456 units was up 14.5% from last September for an increase of 18,765 units. Compared to August, the top 10 markets’ annual permitting total was little changed (-0.7%). In addition to the expanding top 10 and the gateway markets mentioned, other markets with significant increases in annual units permitted in September were Kansas City (+2,187 units), West Palm Beach (+1,932 units), College Station-Bryan, TX (+1,762 units), Tacoma (+1,712 units) and Fort Worth (+1,672 units). Orlando (-4,572 units) led for annual permitting decreases, followed by Dallas and Houston. Significant decreases occurred in Columbus, OH (-2,911 units), Riverside-San Bernardino (-2,162 units), San Diego (-2,100 units) and Lakeland-Winter Haven, FL (-1,995 units). Permitting by Place Below the metro level, eight of August’s top 10 permit-issuing places returned to this month’s list with the first five remaining in order. The list of top individual permitting places (cities, towns, boroughs, and unincorporated counties) generally includes the principal city of some of the most active metro areas. The city of Los Angeles again led the nation for multifamily permitting at the local level with New York’s three most active boroughs returning among the top five. The city of Phoenix also placed in the top five while the city of Fort Worth jumped to #6 in September from #10 last month. The cities of Austin and Atlanta each slipped one spot as the cities of Columbus and Houston fell out of the top 10 entirely. The cities of Miami and Denver joined the top 10 list this month, permitting about 5,500 units apiece. Among the top 10 metros for multifamily permitting, Dallas, Houston, Washington, DC and Raleigh/Durham were not represented on the top 10 list of permitting places, although the core cities of Dallas, Houston, Raleigh and Durham were among the top 20 places. Washington, DC’s multifamily permitting was spread diversely around that metro’s area. items.title: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter
items.description: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter October 30, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private fixed investment in student dormitories rose 2.6% in the third quarter of 2026, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $3.8 billion. This gain marked a second consecutive quarterly increase, despite continued pressures from elevated interest rates. On a year-over-year basis, investments in dorms increased 1.1%. Private fixed investment in student housing experienced a surge after the Great Recession, as college enrollment increased from 17.2 million in 2006 to 20.4 million in 2011. However, during the pandemic, private fixed investment in student housing declined drastically from $4.4 billion (SAAR) in the last quarter of 2019 to $3.1 billion in the second quarter of 2021. According to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center , college enrollment fell by 3.6% in the fall of 2020 and by 3.1% in the fall of 2021. The latest preliminary data indicated that college enrollment held steady in fall 2026 compared with the previous year. Since the pandemic, private fixed investment in dorms has rebounded alongside a gradual recovery in college enrollments. Effective in-person learning requires college students to return to campuses, boosting the student housing sector. Still, demographic trends are reshaping the outlook for student housing. The U.S. faces slower growth in the college-age population as birth rates declined following the Great Recession. Furthermore, changing perceptions towards the value of a college degree as a guaranteed pathway to job security are all contributing to an “enrollment cliff”. items.title: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity?
items.description: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity? Many owners face the challenge of bringing more money into their deal. Sometimes, the cost may outweigh the benefits. Published Oct. 30, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . These days, it feels like you can find a stat to support just about anything you want. Think inflation isn’t an issue? If you watch the Sunday political shows long enough, someone probably has numbers to support that notion. On the other side, there’s probably someone who can tell you that the third-quarter U.S. real gross domestic product growth of 3.4% is a mirage. Think Brian Schottenheimer isn’t getting enough out of the Dallas Cowboys? (Spoiler alert: he isn’t, despite this week's win.) The folks at Pro Football Focus probably have something to back those claims. The same is true in multifamily. Since I started covering this sector, the number of studies, surveys and indexes that fill my inbox each day seems to have quadrupled … at least. I delete most of these research projects or studies because much of this “research” is sent under the guise of pitching products. However, I do look at certain reports and even seek others out. As more loans face issues in the apartment industry, I recently went to CRED iQ’s website to get an idea of the size of the maturity wall. There I found something that caught my eye — an article saying nearly 33% of maturing apartment debt needs a cash infusion to refinance. At first blush, that number felt, well, kind of low, given everything that I’ve been reading about maturity walls and refinance risk. Reading further on the CRED iQ website, I learned that the firm resized every multifamily loan in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and commercial mortgage-backed securities deals maturing between October 2026 and December 2028. Of that $136 billion in debt, 23% of the loans and 31% of the balance can’t refinance without an equity infusion of roughly $6.8 billion. The good news for apartment owners is that money is available to fill that gap. The bad news: It’s getting more expensive. Earlier this year, Maximiliane Leachman, vice chair of CBRE’s debt and structured finance group, told me refinancing is becoming harder for some borrowers. At one point, these lenders may have wanted 1% to 3% of the loan balance for an extension. Now, many could be looking for 10%. “We’re all waiting for the shoe to drop at the end of this year as those borrowers come back for the second time to that debt fund for another modification,” Leachman said. “It will be interesting to see how many of those go back.” But costs aren’t the only issues owners must weigh when deciding whether to bring additional capital into their deals. In a recent conversation, Michael Lynd, CEO of Kairoi Residential, raised another concern: whether refinancing is worth the cost to existing equity holders. “The question that I have when I look at a lot of these refinances is the cost of that refinance is not great for your existing equity,” Lynd said. “If rent growth doesn’t show up in that first six to nine months or a year, then you have a chance of further impairing the equity value that isn't in place.” Lynd thinks a lot of groups are making decisions that might not be in their investors’ best interests by holding on to properties rather than selling them because they don’t want a negative trade on their record. Alternatively, they may want to delay a sale to raise additional capital. “I see it happening all over the place,” Lynd said. “You can get a loan, but should you take that loan? Is that the best risk-adjusted decision for your equity?” If the answer is no and if the market doesn’t snap back, those firms might be doing their investors a disservice. Still, some owners may find data showing refinancing is the best option. And it could be. But just because you can find the data to say something doesn’t make it so. items.title: Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home
items.description: Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home Published on October 30th, 2026 by Kynsay Hunt Redfin today launched Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America , a creative franchise on Redfin.com bringing America's history to life through the remarkable homes and people that helped shape the nation. The franchise invites everyone to explore iconic homes through immersive digital experiences and free public events, starting at Philadelphia’s Betsy Ross House on November 7. From today, Redfin is celebrating America's 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America. With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide. The series debuts with two properties: The Betsy Ross House in Philadelphia: A landmark associated with the creation of the American flag and the story of a pioneering craftswoman and entrepreneur whose work became part of the nation's identity. 1892 Bishop’s Palace in Galveston, Texas: A one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition. Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027. “America's story isn't just written in history books. It's written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.” The Betsy Ross House: A Home Woven into the American Story Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America's founding. The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades. The home's remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning. Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms. 1892 Bishop’s Palace: A Remarkable Gilded Age Home Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923. Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa. The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south. Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition. Redfin will highlight iconic American homes through the end of 2027. items.title: UK Budget Risks Deterring Sovereign Wealth Funds From Real Estate
items.description: The budget is out, and the property industry has concerns. UK Chancellor John Healey avoided a bond-market shock with his “breathing space” budget , and the immediate financial-market reaction was reassuring. Gilt yields did not spike, avoiding an outcome that could have pushed financing costs up even further. However, investors were left waiting for measures capable of bringing borrowing costs down and stimulating new development. The budget also delivered limited progress on development viability, while business rates measures offered some relief to high street occupiers without delivering the structural reform sought by many property owners. But new proposed tax rules for sovereign investors, which threaten to make the UK less attractive to global property capital, caused a sharp intake of breath. Flickr/House of Commons Chancellor John Healey succeeded in placating bond markets, but the property sector raised concerns over sovereign taxes. The government has launched a consultation over its proposal to replace the largely noncodified sovereign immunity from direct taxation with a statutory regime from 1 January 2029. Certain UK property income and capital gains would become taxable, although the reforms include bespoke access to the real estate investment trust regime, with a 15% tax rate on qualifying property income distributions. State-operated overseas pension funds and certain investment management activities would remain exempt. The government claimed the reforms would improve transparency and provide greater certainty for sovereign investors, but many in the property industry worry it could weaken the UK's appeal to investors. “It’s a really unhelpful change,” Real Estate:UK Assistant Director of Finance Rachel Kelly said. She said the proposal introduces additional costs for a significant source of real estate investment while development viability is already under severe pressure. Sovereign wealth funds invested £6.2B in UK property from 2021 to 2024, according to a March report from BPF and CoStar . Although the proposed REIT arrangements and transitional provisions offer some flexibility, the new 15% rate would be a significant increase for qualifying sovereign investors accustomed to paying no tax. It also adds an onerous process. “In addition to the actual additional cost now of investing in the UK for those investors, there will be huge complexity in terms of having to restructure their investments, and there will be a lot of work for some to change how they're structured,” Kelly said. The implications extend beyond the funds themselves. Sovereign wealth funds frequently invest alongside other capital providers, meaning changes to their investment structures could affect co-investors and joint ventures too, Moorfield CEO Charles Ferguson-Davie said. He said the reforms risk sending the wrong signal. “There aren’t that many groups that will deploy over £500M, over a billion,” Ferguson-Davie said. “If they’re going to be less active as a result of having to pay tax, who’s going to step in and invest that money instead?” CBRE Investment Management is looking to understand the rules in more detail during the consultation, Director Alex Lund said. But he expressed optimism that the policy won’t decimate investment. “For any market looking to attract overseas capital ... taxes and the need for a level playing field for domestic and international investors are very important,” he said. “But many investors are already in the UK, which is a large, deep and transparent market, so we would remain positive while looking at the consultation carefully.” Ferguson-Davie said the wider economic benefits of attracting large-scale investment should be part of the government's calculations, rather than focusing solely on the tax revenue generated. He said the string of regulatory or tax burdens added to the private rental sector over the last few budgets show the danger in the government’s thinking. “You can understand the political motivation, but it has already led to a lot of sales and exits from the market,” Ferguson-Davie said. “I'm not sure it's all necessarily ending up benefiting the renter.” Instead, supply and development have both fallen, and that pushes rents up. He said the new budget will encourage the sale of buy-to-lets, which could benefit the institutional build-to-rent sector — but it doesn’t actually solve any problems. “What the BTR community needs, indeed the housing sector needs, is more incentives to help bring down the cost of development,” he said. “If we're going to have a meaningful change in terms of new houses delivered for sale and for rent, we need the regulatory and tax burden reduced, because otherwise it's just going to get worse.” BTR construction starts have fallen 63% in the last year, with only 4,696 groundbreakings in September, versus 12,674 the year prior, according to Savills data for RE:UK . “Investors needed more than a pause in policy changes,” Kelly said. The budget's business rates package provided more immediate support for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses. However, Kelly said the chancellor again failed to deliver meaningful long-term reform. While the absence of another proposed surcharge on higher-value commercial property was welcome, RE:UK has called for the existing surcharge to be repealed and the tax system changed to make investment and refurbishment more attractive. items.title: New Trump housing order targets mortgage and title insurers – Insurance Business
items.description: New Trump housing order targets mortgage and title insurers A White House plan to pull private mortgage insurance off loans sooner, and to let refinancing borrowers skip the lender's title policy, affects two insurance lines that say they already help keep costs down PROPERTY By Stephen Owens Oct 25, 2026 Share Mortgage insurers and title underwriters are the latest targets of the White House's pre-election push on housing costs. President Donald Trump on Oct. 22 signed an executive order, Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People , that leans on the Federal Housing Finance Agency to squeeze costs out of the mortgage process. Two of its four main provisions deal with insurance: a pilot to cancel mortgage insurance premiums ahead of schedule, and a permanent version of FHFA's experiment letting some refinances skip the traditional lender's title policy, according to the White House fact sheet . The rest of the order sets up a federal task force on factory-built housing and tells the Agriculture and Veterans Affairs departments to cut rates on their direct home loans. FHFA Director Bill Pulte called it "the greatest Housing Executive Order in History" on X. The fact sheet, however, sets no equity thresholds, no start dates and no estimate of how many loans would qualify, so mortgage insurers, title underwriters and agents can't yet tell how much business is at stake. Read next: Why home insurance prices are quietly becoming a 2026 midterm flashpoint Mortgage insurers say cancellation rules already exist The mortgage insurance piece would have Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac use automated valuation models to recheck home values on loans they own from time to time, then drop the coverage once a borrower appears to have built enough equity, according to Mortgage Professional America's breakdown of the order . Servicers would have to tell borrowers when cancellation might be possible. The pilot covers only loans originated after it launches. Borrowers already paying premiums would not benefit directly. Mortgage insurers point out that borrowers already have cancellation rights. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, borrower-paid coverage on a conventional loan must end automatically once the balance hits 78% of the home's original value, and borrowers can ask to cancel at 80%, with some able to qualify on the strength of home price gains if conditions are met, according to U.S. Mortgage Insurers (USMI) , the trade group whose members include Enact, Essent, MGIC, National MI and Radian. USMI President Seth Appleton welcomed the focus on costs and said the industry was already lowering them. "Private MI is designed to be temporary, and the system already works much the way the order envisions, because when MI is cancelled, a borrower's monthly payment goes down," he said in the group's statement. USMI's statement describes the order as telling FHFA to consider a pilot, not to launch one. The group says premium rates have fallen 25% since 2017, that more than 800,000 buyers used private coverage in 2025, two-thirds of them first-timers, and that its members insure more than $1.6 trillion in mortgages. Insurers have paid over $62 billion in claims since 2008 that would otherwise have hit the government-sponsored enterprises, lenders and investors, USMI said. The pilot could also affect pricing. Mortgage insurance is priced on how long an insurer expects to keep collecting premiums. Some industry voices warned that a program clipping off late-life, low-risk loans could push insurers to build that lost income into pricing on new business, MPA reported . The order comes during a strong year for mortgage insurers. New insurance written across the six active private insurers (Arch, Enact, Essent, MGIC, NMI and Radian) hit a multi-year high in the second quarter of 2026, with strong credit performance, according to Milliman's quarterly market update . Read next : Old Republic prevails as Massachusetts court rejects title coverage expansion Title waiver pilot would become permanent For title underwriters, the order expands a program their trade group has opposed since 2024. The title acceptance pilot dates to March 2024, when the Biden-era FHFA approved waiving the lender's title policy, or an attorney opinion letter, on certain low-risk refinances where there is confidence the property is free of prior liens, according to a statement from then-Director Sandra Thompson . Fannie Mae launched it in November 2024 with Doma Title Insurance and added Westcor Land Title Insurance Co. in July 2025. Pulte said in June that Fannie would grow it. The order would make the program permanent and broaden it. The order directs FHFA to lift the current 80% loan-to-value cap on eligibility, bring in more title-assessment providers and scrap the geographic limits, according to MPA's reading of the text. It also calls for waiving appraisals and income re-verification on limited cash-out refinances that cut a borrower's monthly payment. The American Land Title Association responded the same day, warning that any cost-cutting push must keep protections for homeowners and their property rights in place rather than shift risk to consumers and taxpayers. In 2024, ALTA called the original pilot a political gesture that offered a false promise of savings. Analysts expect a limited effect for now. Analysts at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods wrote in an Oct. 21 note that refinances account for only about 7% of title premiums, so the earnings hit should be modest while the program stays refi-only. They said the risk would be greater if the waiver ever reached purchase loans, where there is no scalable substitute for a title policy. Refinance volume is low with 30-year rates above 7%, but a rate drop would quickly enlarge the pool of loans eligible for a waiver, and the order would also remove the program's geographic limits. This deceleration in supply growth occurred at the same time as a decline in absorption in recent months, keeping the vacancy rate flat for the third quarter in a row. Rent trends have been mixed in recent periods. items.description: Realpage Economy Express Episode 74 by Arben Skivjani Posted October 30, 2026 in Insights The Fed held rates steady, but two dissenters wanted a hike now, and strong growth and rising inflation are keeping a December increase firmly on the table. The Federal Reserve held rates steady in a 10-to-2 vote, with both dissenters wanting an immediate quarter-point hike. Its statement also upgraded growth to strong and called inflation still elevated, while Warsh declined to commit on December until he sees more data. Fed funds futures now put the odds of a December hike at about 82%, down slightly after Thursday's data but higher than a week ago. Thursday's GDP report showed the economy grew 3.4% last quarter, faster than expected, with investment doing more of the lifting than consumers. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose 3.6% from a year ago in September, with core climbing to 3.1% and prices jumping 0.5% in a single month. Income and spending figures for September show take-home pay fell after inflation and spending went nowhere, with gasoline taking the biggest bite. Consumer surveys diverged, as Conference Board confidence jumped while University of Michigan sentiment barely moved and respondents there expect inflation near 5% over the next year. The National Association of Realtors reported pending home sales at the lowest level on record, as mortgage rates remain above 7% and buyers stay on the sidelines. Housing starts data show apartment starts down about 26% from a year ago, though permits picked up in September, suggesting some builders are lining up projects for later. items.description: Rocket Companies on Thursday reported a third-quarter profit of $709 million, reversing a loss from a year ago as the Detroit-based mortgage lender expanded revenue and gained market share in purchase and refinance lending. The company reported net income of $709 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a net loss of $124 million a year earlier and a second-quarter 2026 net income of $229 million. Net total revenue nearly doubled year over year to $3.28 billion, up from $1.7 billion, while adjusted revenue rose to $2.57 billion, up from $1.87 billion. Adjusted net income fell to $419 million from $441 million in Q2 2026, and adjusted EBITDA declined to $748 million from Q2's $766 million. Mortgage production also slowed, with closed origination volume falling to $43.6 billion, down from $49.1 billion. The sequential decline in adjusted earnings came as mortgage production slowed from the second quarter, even as the company reported a slightly higher gain-on-sale margin. Rocket chief financial officer Brian Brown anticipated the slowdown during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings call, saying he expected Q3 to be “smaller than the second,” a contraction not seen in the industry since 2022. He cited rates above 6.8% and rising inflation expectations as key challenges. “Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” CEO Varun Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage , and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.” During the company's earnings call on Thursday afternoon, Krishna addressed the broader market. "Here's the truth about tough markets: They don't lie," he said. "They strip everything down to what's real. Who has the capital to keep investing? Whose model works in any cycle? Who can win their clients back? And who can move fast when it counts? This quarter did all of this." Brown said during the call that the company estimates its purchase market share approached 6.5% in Q3 2026, up from 6.2% in Q2 2026. Its refinance share reached 15.5%, compared with 14.3% from April through June. Mortgage production and servicing Rocket closed $43.6 billion in mortgage originations in the third quarter, down from $49.1 billion in Q2. Net rate-lock volume fell to $40.4 billion from $47 billion over the same period. The company’s total gain-on-sale margin edged up to 2.54% from 2.48% in Q2. Excluding correspondent lending , Rocket closed $33.5 billion in mortgage volume during the third quarter. Direct-to-consumer lending accounted for $24.6 billion, while wholesale channel Rocket Pro generated $9 billion. The correspondent channel contributed $10.1 billion in closed volume. Rocket’s mortgage servicing portfolio remained steady at about $2 trillion in unpaid principal balance across 9.1 million loans. The company sold mortgage servicing rights tied to $23 billion in unpaid principal balance during Q3, generating $379 million in proceeds. That was down from $53 billion in MSR sales and $795 million in proceeds in Q2. Rocket retained subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the servicing rights sold in the third quarter, compared with nearly 80% in Q2. Total liquidity rose to $11.4 billion at the end of Q3, up from $11.2 billion at the end of the prior quarter. The figure includes $2.7 billion in cash, $2.5 billion in undrawn credit lines and $6.2 billion in available servicing-rights and advance lines. Rocket said its combined servicing portfolio following the Mr. Cooper integration continued to support borrower recapture, with the company reaching its highest recapture levels to date. During Q3, Rocket continued to expand its use of artificial intelligence and its partnerships with real estate companies. The company said it pulled credit on nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer loan volume before borrowers spoke with a loan officer, compared with none a year earlier. Digital mortgage applications accounted for more than 40% of retail refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of nondigital leads. AI voice technology handled 65% of inbound servicing calls, resolving more than half without human assistance. Rocket also reported growth in its real estate partnerships. Redfin visitors who clicked to begin a mortgage transaction increased 50% year over year, while Redfin’s contribution to Rocket’s refinance leads more than doubled in Q3. Listings tied to its Compass partnership reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in Q2. In September, Rocket Mortgage adopted VantageScore 4.0 as its preferred credit scoring model for eligible loans. The company said its testing indicated qualifying borrowers could save an average of $1,600 in closing costs. Rocket Pro launched Orbit in October , offering eligible purchase borrowers same-day conditional approval and a 12-business-day timeline to clear-to-close. The company also extended a Compass pricing credit through the end of 2026. The partnership had generated more than $3 billion in rate locks since February. items.title: Housing’s Share of the Economy Falls Again as It Continues to Face Headwinds
items.description: Housing’s Share of the Economy Falls Again as It Continues to Face Headwinds October 30, 2026 Jesse Wade No Comments Housing’s share of the economy was 15.7% in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest estimates of GDP produced by the Bureau of Economic Analysis . This share is down from 15.8% in the second quarter and down from 16.0% a year ago. Residential construction, measured by residential fixed investment, fell for the sixth time over the past eight quarters. The more cyclical home building and remodeling component–residential fixed investment (RFI)–was 3.6% of GDP, even with the previous quarter. The second component, housing services, was 12.2% of GDP, also even with the previous quarter. The graph below plots the share for housing services and RFI, along with housing’s total share of nominal GDP. Housing service expenditures are much less volatile when compared to RFI due to the cyclical nature of RFI. Historically, RFI has averaged roughly 5% of GDP, while housing services have averaged between 12% and 13%, for a combined 17% to 18% of GDP. These shares tend to vary over the business cycle. However, the housing share of GDP lagged during the post-Great Recession period due to underbuilding, particularly in the single-family sector. Residential Fixed Investment In the third quarter, RFI subtracted 12 basis points from the headline GDP growth rate. This reversed the 10 basis points that RFI added to GDP growth in the second quarter. RFI declined 3.3% in the third quarter on an annualized basis to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $1.17 trillion, down from $1.18 trillion in the second quarter. RFI can be split into two segments: structures and equipment. Residential structure investment not only consists of new single-family and multifamily units but also includes manufactured homes, improvements, and dormitories. Residential equipment, which accounts for under 2% of total RFI, consists of furniture or household appliances that are purchased by landlords for rental to tenants. Real private investment in structures fell 3.6%, while investment in residential equipment rose 9.9%. Breaking down the components of residential structures, single-family RFI fell 5.0%, while multifamily RFI rose 0.3%. Permanent site structure RFI, which is made up of single-family and multifamily RFI, fell 3.8%. The “other structures” RFI category was down 3.4% in the third quarter. This component consists primarily of manufactured homes, improvements, and dormitories. On a seasonally adjusted annual basis in the third quarter, private investment in permanent site structures was at $514.9 billion, while other structures totaled $635.4 billion. While RFI has declined over the past year, nonresidential fixed investment has grown substantially. In the third quarter, nonresidential fixed investment grew 12.7%, the seventh straight quarter of growth. Most of this investment is in nonresidential equipment, as it grew 20.9% in the third quarter. This was led by investment in information processing equipment, specifically computer equipment. Nonresidential structure investment rose 5.4% in the third quarter, led by commercial and health care structure investment. Notably, investment in manufacturing structures fell by double digits for the seventh straight quarter, with a decline of 15.3% on an annualized rate in the third quarter. Housing Services The second impact of housing on GDP is the measure of housing services. Similar to RFI, housing services consumption can be broken into two components. The first component, housing, includes gross rents paid by renters, owners’ imputed rent (an estimate of how much it would cost to rent owner-occupied units), rental value of farm dwellings, and group housing. The inclusion of owners’ imputed rent is necessary from a national income accounting approach, because without this measure, increases in homeownership would result in declines in GDP. The second component, household utilities, is composed of consumption expenditures on water supply, sanitation, electricity, and gas. For the third quarter, housing services represented 12.2% of the economy or $4.0 trillion on a seasonally adjusted annual basis. Real housing services expenditure rose 2.8% at an annual rate in the third quarter. Real personal consumption expenditure for housing grew 1.1%, while real household utilities expenditures rose 15.3%. Personal consumption expenditure (PCE) on housing services is the largest component of PCE, making up 18.0% in the third quarter. The second largest component of PCE is health care services, at 17.0%. Expenditure on services was $15.4 trillion on a seasonally adjusted annual basis in the third quarter, more than double the expenditure on goods ($6.9 trillion). housing share of gdp , U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) Prev Previous PCE Inflation Accelerated in September Next Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter Next Leave a Reply Cancel reply Your email address will not be published. items.title: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q
items.description: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published October 29, 2026, 7:27 p.m. EDT | Updated October 29, 2026, 8:21 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Pennymac posted its lowest mortgage origination and acquisition volume since the first quarter of 2024. Supporting Data: While the company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, its servicing pretax income rose to $99 million. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. PennyMac Financial Services is making deeper cost cuts after its originations fell 30% this summer. The lender and servicer will slash $160 million in annualized operating expenses in the coming months as it anticipates higher-for-longer rates, it said Thursday. That expands on cuts that began this summer in response to some of the worst mortgage market conditions this decade. Processing Content While the company remained well in the black for the third quarter, its combined origination segment volume of $24.4 billion was its lowest mark since the first quarter of 2024. Chairman and CEO David Spector, in an earnings call Thursday evening, described the current landscape as "one of the most constrained origination environments our industry has seen since 2023." Pennymac didn't provide additional details about staff reductions . For the third quarter, Pennymac posted a $29 million profit, surpassing the $22 million net income in the second quarter. That was still a fraction of the $181.5 million profit Pennymac posted at the same time last year. Although elevated rates and heightened competition battered origination performance, the company highlighted stronger income in servicing, and green shoots in artificial intelligence advancements. Inside the numbers The company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, after marks of $38 million and $122.9 million in the prior quarter and year-ago periods, respectively. Servicing pretax income meanwhile rose to $99 million, soaring from $22 million in the second quarter but falling from $157 million a year ago. Pennymac also agreed to sell $29 billion in unpaid principal balance of low-rate conventional mortgage servicing rights, it said. It plans to redeploy the $490 million in proceeds to reduce higher-cost debt, and repurchase common shares. The servicing book ended the quarter slightly up around $737 billion. Revenues fell to end the period at $469 million, declines of 6% quarterly and 26% annually. Executive outlook Company leaders expanded on origination trends, with Pennymac posting greater consumer direct margins with more closed-end second lien volume. Spector also suggested competitive pressures from the government-sponsored enterprises' cash window for smaller brokerages, and the industry leaders' aggressive pricing. "We're picking and choosing our spots, and maintaining market share, and not really getting too caught up in market share at levels that are just not sustainable or that one can rationalize," said Spector. Pennymac also touted its AI advancements, noting that its tech spending is coming down. The lender has 22 proprietary AI agents live in production and is developing 17 more, while its proprietary AI voice agent supported over 1,600 rate locks in the third quarter. "This will allow us to maintain lean operation in today's constrained environment, while ensuring substantial operating leverage when origination volumes normalize," Spector said of the company's AI prowess. What's ahead The firm also announced some executive moves, as President and Chief Mortgage Banking Officer Doug Jones will retire next June. Chief Strategy Officer Kevin Ryan will be elevated to chief financial officer in January, while current CFO Daniel Perotti will remain in that role through the end of the year. Pennymac's Cenlar deal, which will bring its servicing book past $1 trillion , is now expected to close early next year, as executives said they're waiting on one remaining state approval. items.title: The housing market gets a positive Fed day for a change
items.description: On Wednesday we got an October surprise: the Fed day was eerily calm, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh looking comfortable on stage and offering a slightly dovish take on the future — if a few things improve. I believe the Fed wants to take back all the interest rate cuts from last year, and then they can assess what is happening in the economy. Of course, the Iran conflict and Trade War 2.0 have complicated their job, but today, given that markets were at one point pricing in five to six rate hikes, was a positive day. Last I checked, the 10-year was at 5.02%, down after Google reported a bad quarter. The Fed's press statement was short and simple, but two things caught my attention. 1. The economy is strong vs. solid First, the Fed chose to use the word "strong" instead of "solid" on purpose to signal it won’t cut rates and will continue reversing last year's interest rate cuts while inflation stays above target. “ Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Warsh said jobless claims data remain low and that the Fed fully intends to bring inflation back to the 2% target, no compromise. He also said the Fed will hold one fewer voting meeting in 2027 and two fewer meetings in 2028; this approach might leave the Fed open to more 50-basis-point cuts or hikes. However, that is another story for another time. 2. Warsh liked the market drama against AI I got a strong sense that Warsh liked the market getting more restrictive and that we even saw some AI companies shed some blood recently. My theme in the HousingWire Daily podcast lately borrows from The Predator movie: the AI god king can bleed — and that it means you can kill it. I think Warsh was implying no company is invincible, and that if the market gets more restrictive, things can change, as they recently did. He also talked about how the 10-year yield rolled over even though oil prices have been elevated this month. I believe the 10-year yield rollover is more market-driven, as the 10-year was pricing in more rate hikes than the Fed was targeting at the time. The term premium on the 10-year yield was elevated as it headed to the October high. If the 10-year had closed over the key level of 5.35%, bond yields had the potential to rise much higher, faster, as the markets would be pricing in a much more aggressive Fed rate hike cycle, but, smartly, they chose not to go that route. Warsh seems to enjoy that everyone is taking the Fed seriously and that the markets have already done a lot of the work for them. This reaffirms my assumption that all they want to do is take back the rate cuts from last year and then reassess what is going on. One side note was that Fed Governor Lisa Cook — who is usually a dove — voted to raise rates, which I 100% believe was a trolling tactic on her part since Trump still wants to fire her . All in all, it wasn’t a bad day; the 10-year yield is above 5% still today, but considering the market was trying to price in five to six rate hikes, and there hasn’t been any end to the conflict or the trade war, I consider this a victory for the month of October. For housing, the worst-case scenario has been averted and we bought some time, giving space for the conflict to end and the trade war to cool off a bit. What I am hoping for is that we get some more clarity on both of those two items, and then the Fed can make the rate hike cycle just a few rate hikes, and then we'll take it from there. items.title: Enterprise Bank & Trust exits mortgage industry, cites scale
items.description: Enterprise Bank & Trust exits mortgage industry, cites scale By Colin McNamara Published October 29, 2026, 5:59 p.m. EDT 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Why depository banks continue to exit the mortgage industry. What's at Stake: Local homebuyers seeking mortgage options as more regional depositories exit the origination space. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Another depository is exiting the mortgage industry in order to cut expenses, continuing a trend that has persisted through the current high-rate environment . Processing Content Enterprise Bank & Trust, headquartered in Clayton, Missouri, confirmed the move on its third-quarter earnings call last week, saying it looked at multiple areas of business in the company that were subscale. "We also recently announced that we're exiting the mortgage business as it relates to an originator," said Jim Lally, CEO of Enterprise Financial Services Corp., on the call. "So we're taking expenses out where we're not adding a great deal of value and really can scale." Jim Lally, CEO of Enterprise Financial Services Corp. Enterprise joins Michigan-based Northpointe Bank as depositories to leave the mortgage space in October. Northpointe announced it sold its distributed retail and consumer direct channels to CMG Financial , an independent mortgage bank. Northpointe Chairman and CEO Chuck Williams said in an earnings call last week that volumes could no longer carry the overhead of mortgage operations, citing economic headwinds. Another executive said the deal doesn't involve the transfer of loans and similar assets. The bank will retain other lending activity, including a mortgage purchase program comparable to warehouse lending. Under the terms of the agreement, CMG will pay Northpointe 15 basis points on any first-lien mortgage originations closed through the mortgage origination channels until Dec. 31, 2028, the bank announced in a press release this week. Unlike the Northpointe transaction, Enterprise has not announced a buyer or referral partner for its mortgage business. Why banks should stay in mortgage Despite recent examples, Rich Swerbinsky, executive director of the Ohio Mortgage Bankers Association and founder of Upward & Onward Consulting, said banks that previously left the mortgage industry, or never conducted business in it, have been rethinking their decision. At the American Bankers Association's annual conference, multiple banking executives made the case for staying in mortgage without building a 40-person department, Swerbinsky said. "I think the wind's at the back of depositories right now," he wrote in his newsletter, Swerbs Blurbs, Wednesday. "Capital rules are loosening, portfolio lending is back in play, talent is moving, and all this AI has people craving local, in-person relationships. Consumers need more options, especially local ones." Enterprise's third-quarter results In addition to shutting down its mortgage business, the company withdrew from some banking activities in markets, particularly in the West, where it lacked interest to properly compete, Lally said in the call. The moves come after Enterprise posted continued growth in its broader lending business. The company recorded a 3.8% quarterly and 6.6% annual increase in total loans to $12.3 billion but a net income of $42.4 million, which was down 6.2% year over year. items.title: Office Recovery Moving Faster Than Expected, CoStar Finds
items.description: American office buildings are filling up faster than previously predicted, with a lack of new construction expected to drive vacancy lower through the next year. Unsplash/Khara Woods CoStar Group revised its office predictions through the end of next year to reflect rising demand for increasingly hard-to-find high-quality space. The ubiquitous online real estate marketplace now expects lower vacancy rates due in large part to an all-but-dead construction pipeline. “The latest forecast calls for a continuation of the slow-but-steady revival, with an ongoing supply-side adjustment offsetting historically weak office demand growth,” Phil Mobley , national director of office analytics at CoStar Group, said in a statement. CoStar projects absorption to be around 20M SF in 2026 and 9M SF in 2027, up from 13M SF and 5M SF, respectively, from its previous forecast released in August. Office vacancy is expected to end the year around 13.6%, just below the previous 13.7% forecast. High-quality properties will continue to drive pricing higher, with CoStar predicting asking rents will climb 2.5% in each of the next few quarters before rising closer to 3% annually. The upward revision to the rent forecast was more to do with a shift in inventory accounting than an expected boost in activity. “The upgraded projection for office rent growth has less to do with the overall reduction in supply caused by the removal of non-competitive space and more to do with the dramatic slowdown in new construction,” Mobley said. CoStar Group The office market has continued to rebound from pandemic-era lows, driven by demand from tech firms and the more general push from tenants into high-quality spaces. Leasing activity totaled 63.8M SF in the third quarter, up 4% from last year and on track to exceed a 2022 record, according to CBRE . Absorption was positive for the 10th consecutive quarter at just under 5M SF at the end of September, with the construction pipeline a paltry 1.5M SF, down 76% from the prior year. Rent growth is accelerating at its fastest pace since 2016, according to CBRE. Analysts at CoStar said the risks on either side of its forecast seemed roughly in balance in terms of probability, but with larger downside risks in terms of size. “Persistent inflation and higher interest rates could slow economic growth further and precipitate additional business cost-cutting even in an environment of continued economic expansion,” Mobley said. “Furthermore, the recent productivity gains evident in knowledge work could accelerate with further adoption of artificial intelligence , resulting in lower demand for some types of knowledge workers.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: CBRE , Colliers , CoStar , CoStar Group , Phil Mobley

Wikimedia Commons/Derrick Coetzee The Guadalupe Quarry The project has been scaled back 33% from an original proposal to one two-story industrial building on previously disturbed quarry land, while the remaining 82 acres would be dedicated to permanent open space. A modern Class-A industrial building would be somewhat of a rarity on the San Francisco Peninsula — 77% of Mid-Peninsula industrial inventory was built prior to 1980, according to JLL researchers. “Our goal has been to thoughtfully balance land conservation and environmental stewardship of the quarry with the growing needs of modern industrial users,” Orchard Partners Managing Partner Tyler Higgins said in a statement. items.description: CCM's VantageScore test saves $2,500; rivals lock FICO deals By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 30, 2026, 4:52 p.m. EDT | Updated October 30, 2026, 5:36 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Find out why some major mortgage lenders are signing on for FICO's bundled pricing and how much another prominent player says VantageScore has been saving them on certain loans. Expert Quote: "A 740 classic FICO isn't necessarily the same risk as a 740 VantageScore loan." — Sandra Thompson, former director, Federal Housing Finance Agency Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Some lenders have signed up for FICO's bundle while another one has found savings in government-sponsored enterprises' unified loan pricing for VantageScore 4.0, highlighting new drivers for how the industry is making choices around credit metrics. Fairway, Movement and Rate reported Friday that they have committed to FICO's bundle , which pledges a price freeze for commitments, while CrossCountry Mortgage found that a 60-day test of VantageScore 4.0 generated an average of $2,500 in savings on some loans. Processing Content "This demonstrates how additional flexibility can translate into meaningful benefits for our customers," Brian Clark, director of product and pricing at CCM, said in a press release, while noting that it's part of broader moves to fully use government-related market options to this end. Brian Clark, CrossCountry Mortgage CCM also is removing a 80% loan-to-value ratio cap it has had as an overlay for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans, allowing some borrowers to exceed this, and also giving borrowers broader access to Department of Veterans Affairs-guaranteed loans. Meanwhile, Rocket Mortgage also has found VS4 offers some advantages in a five-month test of 1.4 million customers, CEO Jay Bray said at Housing Finance Strategies' conference this week. Rocket reported earlier that it would be making VantageScore its default credit metric . "We saw higher approval. We saw customers being able to save money, and so we made the choice to move in that direction for certain pieces of our portfolio," he told listeners to the conference, which HFS broadcast online. Lenders sees a need for both score providers for now VS4 has become more competitive in the GSEs' market since their oversight agency unified the pricing for loans based on it with FICO's longtime industry standard, removing a previous adjustment, but so far lenders are still reporting a need for both credit metrics. "Since VantageScore 4.0 isn't accepted across all programs yet, this approach gives loan officers more flexibility," CCM said in its emailed statement. Executives from Fairway, Rate and Movement all also issued statements that show a persistent need for FICO scores in a press release. "We will continue to evaluate FICO Scores in our wide range of eligible loan products and programs," Stacey Sprain, senior vice president of credit and vendor support at Fairway Home Mortgage, said in one such statement. VantageScore 4.0 and a newer FICO 10T score slated for later enterprise adoption both differ from the latter's traditional credit metric for mortgages in that they both incorporate more data such as borrower payments over time as opposed to a snapshot of the borrower's obligations. While CrossCountry has reported some early savings related to current GSE loan pricing with no differentiation for FICO classic and VS4 scores, former Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Sandra Thompson said this week she had some concerns about it. Ex-officials' take on current loan pricing for scores "The most important aspect of credit modernization is getting the risk pricing of the loans done correctly," Thompson said. "A 740 classic FICO isn't necessarily the same risk as a 740 VantageScore loan," she said during the Housing Finance Strategies conference. Scores the GSEs use in loan pricing have broad impacts for them and their counterparties that Thompson said should be given more consideration before treating them in a unified manner. Sandra Thompson "Capital is absolutely going to be impacted. The mortgage insurers are looking at these numbers as well," Thompson said. Both she and her fellow HFS conference panelist Alanna McCargo, who previously served as president of Ginnie Mae and then later of the Federal Home Loan Bank of San Francisco, called for more data around such implications. "I just think we need to be very careful as this rolls out," McCargo said.
