items.title: In Midterm Toss-Up States of Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Maine, Housing Affordability Is Top of Mind
items.description: As the country heads into the final days before the 2026 midterm elections, housing affordability weighs heavily on many voters’ minds. A recent Pew Research Center poll found that 66% of Americans are “very concerned” about housing costs. And this past July, CNBC’s All-America Economic Survey found that housing affordability is the top concern for Gen Z voters and men aged 18 to 44. That’s likely because Americans are spending more money—and more of their incomes—on housing than they have in recent memory. A 2024 study from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found that nearly half of all Americans—49%—spend more than the recommended 30% of their income on housing. Yet lawmakers and voters remain divided on how to ease the economic burden so many Americans now face. Is it an issue of building more housing or backing more programs to subsidize rents and mortgages? Will raising wages solve the problem, or will creating more tenant protections offer relief? Or is the answer some combination of all of the above? That's why, ahead of the 2026 midterms, Realtor.com® examined the housing issues animating voters in the four states that Decision Desk HQ has deemed Senate race toss-ups, with no clear leader in the polls: Maine , Iowa , Ohio , and Texas . The goal was to understand better how housing issues are animating voters and what residents hope lawmakers will do once elected. Despite radically different local environments, several common themes emerged: People feel that owning a home has become increasingly out of reach. They worry about people on the lowest end of the economic spectrum. They are also skeptical that an election will really change much. Read on to learn what housing advocates and average citizens across Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Maine want lawmakers to focus on after the electionn. Maine voters are a mix of newcomers and longtime landowners In the race for Maine's Senate seat, Democrat Troy Jackson is narrowly favored to defeat longtime incumbent Susan Collins , a Republican. Both agree that private equity investment in residential properties was a major problem in the state, though they don’t necessarily agree on how to solve it. Jackson criticized Collins for voting against an amendment from Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH) that would support building 7 million new homes and expanding affordable housing opportunities. Collins has criticized Jackson for claiming two homes as primary residences for tax benefits. Dan Martin, 41, and his family moved to Freeport, ME , from New Jersey five years ago, trading proximity to New York City for more space and a better quality of life. He’s one of more than 126,000 people who have moved to Maine since 2020, and he says he was struck by the disparity in housing access in the state. “Landowners here own a lot of land, and they’re often unwilling to give it up,” he says. “And that’s fine, but it does create a disparity in what’s available. “We have a wide breadth of wealthy generational Mainers alongside Somalian refugees," he continues. "And we don’t have enough housing—low-income housing for those folks." The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that Maine has a shortage of 20,000 rental homes for extremely low-income residents. Wages in the state also haven’t kept up with housing costs. At the state minimum wage of $15.10 an hour, a worker must put in 67 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment at a fair market price of $1,323 a month, according to NLIHC . Loading... The town hall in Bangor, ME, is equipped with voting booths for early midterm voting on Oct. 16, 2026. Americans voting in the Nov. 3 elections will decide who controls Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency. AFP via Getty Images Ohioans want affordable and 'attainable' housing On Tuesday, Republican incumbent John Husted faces Democrat challenger Sherrod Brown in the Ohio race for U.S. Senate. Brown, a former Senator, narrowly leads in the polls, according to Decision Desk . Hu s ted ’s campaign has stressed increasing the housing supply, cutting federal regulations, and enabling private investment rather than direct government funding. Brown favors lowering housing costs, expanding inventory, and protecting affordable housing. Sonya Fix is a professor at Columbus College of Art and Design in Columbus, OH , and has lived in the city on and off for most of her life. She purchased her home in 2018, but says that many of her fellow 40-something friends are struggling to do so now. "I’ve seen friends who are even in better positions than me not be able to buy a house. All of a sudden, during the [COVID-19] pandemic, everyone wanted to buy a house, and rates started going up. So I consider myself pretty lucky to have bought what I did." Some of those friends "might have owned a house at one point but got divorced and have been renting. You know, it's just, it's really hard to reenter the market as a buyer now because houses are so expensive." Some of her friends who are renting are also feeling the squeeze. "I am just absolutely shocked. I have no clue how working-class, lower-income, or even lower-middle-class families who have to rent are doing it," she says. Apartments that once rented for $500 to $600 a month now cost twice as much. Fix would like to see stronger tenant protections, especially since two-bedroom rents in Ohio increased 28% between January 2020 and January 2025, according to the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio . "Especially in Columbus and the surrounding areas, where there's a lot of big tech coming in,” she says. "There has to be rental protections to allow people to stay in their homes as opposed to getting shoved out so that the landlord can get someone with more money." Marcus Roth , communications director of the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio, sees the housing crisis in the state as a multipronged problem, one that’s no longer just an issue for low-income Americans.

items.title: National Inflation Averages Hide Local CRE Opportunities, Marcus & Millichap Says
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | October 29, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter National Inflation Averages Hide Local CRE Opportunities, Marcus & Millichap Says Higher-than-expected September inflation has been driving the CRE narrative of increased cost of capital, along with rising operating and construction expenses. The consumer price index rose 3.7% year-over-year in September, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, while the producer price index for final demand climbed 6.3% A recent Marcus & Millichap video said that the main inflation drivers have been energy prices, up 20.4% year-over- year , and transportation costs, up 7.8%. “But we have to remember that, while we have a national inflation rate, not all states or metros are facing the exact same cost increases,” Marcus & Millichap Senior Vice President John Chang said in the video. Metro-Level Differences Chang pointed out that, on a year-over-year basis, inflation was: 1.3% in Houston, TX 1.9% in Tampa, FL 2.5% in Phoenix, AZ On the other side of the spectrum, inflation stood at: 4.5% in New York, NY 4.7% in San Diego, CA 5.2% in Hawaii Diesel, a primary driver of inflation, shows the same pattern. Nationally, diesel averages about $6.30 per gallon. But the Chang said that diesel ran about $5.60 to $5.80 in North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Texas and Louisiana. Meanwhile, California reached about $8.50 per gallon, with prices in Washington, Oregon, Nevada and Hawaii ranging from about $6.75 to $7.30. "My point here is that national averages don't tell the whole story, and that carries over to commercial real estate," Chang said. Wide Ranges Within Property Types Chang acknowledged that broad trends, including elevated inflation, slowing job creation and rising interest rates, generate CRE headwinds that can impact cap rates. But the opposite is true when digging down to the metro, submarket and asset levels. For example, office cap rates differed, depending on the property: Apartment cap rates also showed a wide range: Chang said that many investors will push higher in the coming months, providing opportunities for investors. In addition, “motivated sellers are already reevaluating their pricing, creating unique investment opportunities," he added. Overall, the national economic and investment headwinds are real. But they can vary when you get down to the market and property level. “At some point, the headwinds will abate,” Chang commented. “As that happens, core commercial real estate drivers like demographics, slowing construction, and pent-up demand will reassert." items.title: SEG Solar Acquires Two Manufacturing Buildings Totaling 1.1 MSF in Tomball, Texas
items.description: SEG Solar Acquires Two Manufacturing Buildings Totaling 1.1 MSF in Tomball, Texas by Taylor Williams October 30, 2026 October 30, 2026 6 TOMBALL, TEXAS —SEG Solar has acquired two manufacturing buildings totaling roughly 1.1 million square feet within Northwest 99 Business Park in Tomball, a northwestern suburb of Houston. Building 2 totals 450,320 square feet and is under construction as a planned conversion into an additional solar module manufacturing facility. Building 3 totals 704,080 square feet and is also under construction to support the company’s distribution operations. Jon Lindenberger and Barkley Peschel of Colliers represented SEG Solar, which previously purchased the 425,360-square-foot Building 1 within the park in 2025, in both transactions. Clay Development owns Northwest 99 Business Park. items.title: Realty Capital Breaks Ground on 289-Unit Apartment Complex in Granbury, Texas
items.description: Realty Capital Breaks Ground on 289-Unit Apartment Complex in Granbury, Texas by Taylor Williams October 30, 2026 October 30, 2026 8 GRANBURY, TEXAS —The multifamily arm of local developer Realty Capital has broken ground on Lofts at Lakeview, a 289-unit apartment complex that will be located in Granbury, about 40 miles southwest of Fort Worth. The property will offer one-, two- and three-bedroom across four buildings. Amenities will include a pool, fitness center, resident clubhouse, coworking space, a sky lounge and outdoor grilling and dining stations. Origin Bank is financing construction of the project, which is slated for an early 2028 completion. items.title: Open houses jump 19% in Houston
items.description: Open houses jump 19% in Houston by Emily Marek October 30, 2026 The Houston Weekly Activity Snapshot from the Houston Association of REALTORS. Houston Realtors held 10,300 open houses during the week ended Oct. 26 — a 19.1% annual increase, according to the Weekly Activity Snapshot from the Houston Association of REALTORS® . New, pending and closed listings all declined, however. New listings decreased 3.2% year over year, with 3,215 homes added to the market, down from 3,322 during the same week in 2025. Pending listings dropped 26.7%, with 1,515 properties going under contract, and closings fell 3.8%, with 1,574 home sales during the week. Meanwhile, property showings and listing views on HAR.com decreased by 6.7% and 10.9%, respectively. items.title: Lantern and Fortress Secure $150 Million Financing to Expand Bluejack Resort Platform
items.description: Live Poll Lantern Asset Management and Fortress Investment Group have closed a $150 million credit facility to support the expansion of Bluejack , a Texas-based private club and residential resort developer. Led by funds managed by Fortress affiliates, the capital will fund infrastructure, amenities, and real estate development across Bluejack’s footprint. The financing follows Lantern’s corporate reorganization of Bluejack and the creation of Bluejack Management Partners, an integrated owner-operator platform overseeing club operations, residential construction, hospitality, and development. Bluejack’s properties include Bluejack National in Montgomery—home to the first Tiger Woods-designed golf course in the U.S.—and Bluejack Ranch, a 914-acre community in Aledo. “We’ve spent the last twelve years proving what Bluejack can be, and now we have the leadership and partners to think much bigger about what comes next,” said Andy Mitchell , chairman and CEO of Bluejack Management Partners and Lantern. “Fortress understands what we’ve built, believes in where we’re going and brings tremendous experience to the table.” Introducing: The POWER 50 Our new program spotlights North Texas executives under 50 shaping the region’s future. Nominations are open through Nov. 13. Learn More SpendRule Secures $4 Million Seed Round Led by Mark Cuban’s Radical Investments Dallas-based AI contract enforcement startup SpendRule has raised $4 million in seed funding led by Mark Cuban ’s Radical Investments, with participation from Zeal Capital Partners. The round brings total funding to $6 million and will support product engineering, expansion into new enterprise verticals, and deeper deployment across healthcare systems. “Companies spend all this time negotiating contracts, but what’s the point if nobody checks whether they’re getting what they paid for? That’s the problem SpendRule is solving,” Cuban said. Founded in 2025, SpendRule provides an automated verification platform that reconciles negotiated contract terms against incoming vendor invoices before payments clear. The platform currently oversees $2.91 billion in annual purchased services spend across 2,187 business relationships for healthcare providers including OSF HealthCare, Kettering Health, MemorialCare, and MUSC Health. Rainier Partners Acquires Richardson-Based Apex Insurance Services Seattle-based private equity firm Rainier Partners has acquired Apex Insurance Services, a managing general agency (MGA) platform serving the Texas non-standard auto insurance market. Headquartered in Richardson, Apex operates five MGA brands: Apollo MGA, Apollo Specialty, Newstar General Agency, Excellent Insurance Services, and Ignition Insurance Services. Founded in 2014, Apex distributes through more than 1,000 independent agent contracts across roughly 2,500 retail locations statewide. With Rainier’s backing, the company plans to expand its footprint in Texas, enter adjacent geographic markets, evaluate new product lines, and pursue add-on acquisitions among personal lines MGAs. “We’ve built an enduring and diversified insurance platform at Apex, and we see significant runway for further expansion in the state of Texas and beyond,” said Apex CEO Bryan Ward. “Rainier’s experience in our industry, as well as their compatible team culture and roll-up-your-sleeves approach to partnership, made us confident they were the right partners for Apex’s next stage of growth.” SAP Selects Addison for Integrated North Texas Regional Headquarters Enterprise software firm SAP will consolidate its North Texas operations into a regional hub at Spectrum Center in Addison. The consolidation brings approximately 1,000 employees from SAP’s Plano office and SAP Concur’s Allen office to 5080 Spectrum Drive. Set to open in mid-2027, the facility will house regional business operations, software development, and a customer experience center showcasing SAP's enterprise software and AI applications. “This new space in Addison is a meaningful moment for our team,” said Michael May, managing director for SAP's U.S. South Market Unit. “It will be a space built around the things that matter most to us: our people, our customers, and our communities. Being able to do that in one of the country’s top innovation and tech talent hubs makes it even more exciting.” The Addison City Council approved an incentive package on Oct. 13 that includes a capital investment grant of up to $500,000, alongside performance milestones. SAP joins a growing cluster of enterprise tech firms along the Lower Dallas North Tollway, including Google, ServiceNow, Tanium, and Hitachi Digital Services. Concurrently, equity partner Arenova Capital increased its equity commitment to $75 million to accelerate the buildout of Aspire’s 10 Gigabit-capable fiber network across Southern California. items.title: Taste Test: Uptown’s $31 Burger
items.description: Live Poll It’s called the White Burger. The name is not a literal description but a multivalent pun, referring to the “white label” custom blend of beef cuts used, the slice of white American cheese, and the chef, Michael White. White has been serving his burger in New York , London, and Washington, D.C. for years now, a casual calling card for a career that also includes Michelin stars at his past restaurants Marea and Ai Fiori. Both remain open, but White left in 2021 to consult on restaurants in New York, Miami, the Bahamas, and now Dallas. Lions Den is a hideaway Italian restaurant in the back of the Stoneleigh Hotel, with wallpapered ceilings, comfortable banquettes, discreet service, and no apostrophe in its name. At night, it serves veal chops, Dover sole, crab bucatini, and oxtail agnolotti. At lunch, it has the $31 White Burger. Here’s what you get. That custom-blended patty is about as thick as a deck of cards, cooked to a textbook medium with pink running through the center, then blanketed with white American. It’s topped very minimally: just caramelized onions and a Dijon-mayo blend at the time of writing. (In summertime, a bacon mushroom marmalade was the condiment of choice.) The bun gets toasted until genuinely crisp—you’ll feel it between your teeth—in contrast to the soft umami pillow of meat, cheese, and onion within. On the side, a pickle has been so thoroughly coated with espelette pepper that it looks like candy. Fries, super-crisp and salted just right, come in a dainty metal cup. This isn’t one of those throw-five-flavors-at-you burgers. It doesn’t need bacon, and it sure has no use for lettuce. It locks in on one ultrasavory frequency of righteous umami beef and cheese, and doesn’t let up. It’s also $31. Yes, it comes with a generous amount of beef. Yes, that beef is wagyu, but the term “wagyu” means less than you think and butchers can get the desired fat content for a burger patty from any breed of cattle. The fries, bun, and caramelized onions speak to a well-trained kitchen brigade, so there is plenty of labor cost on display in the finished burger. Restaurants & Bars How To Read the Steak Menu Is wagyu better? Is Akaushi best? Is anything less than Prime an insult? Here is the truth behind the marketing fluff. By Brian Reinhart | October 8, 2026 | 12:55 pm But everyone has their own standards of value. Many of this magazine’s readers won’t blink. Good things are worth paying for. Others will see the $31 burger as a sign of impending apocalypse. Whatever your view, I can assure you of two things. First, it is not a total reinvention of the burger genre. It’s not bedazzled with truffles, gold leaf, or caviar, nor is it overengineered with cheffy sauces. If you can find a good $17 burger that scratches the same itch, go for it. Second, however, this is a good burger. Maybe you’ll be in Uptown one lunch hour and you’ll be offered free lunch from a generous friend, or a friend who recently spilled a drink in the back of your car and is harboring feelings of guilt. Times like these call for the White Burger. Full disclosure: Lions Den recognized me and presented me with a bill for $0.01. I left a $39.99 tip, which the restaurant processed. If the restaurant had not allowed me to pay, I would have been ethically barred from writing about the meal. I'm glad they did, and I imagine my server is glad, too. items.title: StrongSide, The Show: Owen Newkirk Talks All Things Stars
items.description: Live Poll The Cowboys may have reached a turning point, or they might be set up to spiral. The young Mavericks might be on the upswing, or they could hit growing pains. As for the Stars, well, we know precisely what we’re getting from them: consistency and quality. It’s time for a deep dive about the current standard in the market, so the Mikes brought in Owen Newkirk, currently of DLLS Stars and formerly the team’s pre- and post-game announcer. He talks about the subtle differences in Glen Gulutzan’s second season behind the bench before zooming in on Jake Oettinger’s scalding start to the season, the Jason Robertson negotiations, and how much attention we ought to pay to the reporting that Norris-winning defenseman Zach Werenski could be back in play after all. What’s the best Stars sweater of all time? Which Stars goalie would you want in net for a Game 7? And will Robertson be working here in 2027? Elsewhere, the Mikes take stock of the Cowboys after heading into a softer November schedule. Mike Senior lists some of the many reasons why the Mavericks look so promising out of the gate. And if Jerry Jones and Troy Aikman are publicly talking up the idea of a reunion in the Cowboys’ front office. Let’s peel back the layers of what could be happening here. Tap in for StrongSide, Episode 49! Watch the Full Episode Reading List Mavericks CEO Rick Welts made a sooner-than-expected exit from Dallas. What could that tell us about the team’s upcoming new arena? Bethany Erickson read some tea leaves.
